By Mike Allen · Nov 27, 2026

🕶️ It's Black Friday! Thanks for joining us for this doorbuster edition.

  • Smart Brevity™ count: 1,359 words ... 5 mins. Thanks to Erica Pandey for orchestrating. Edited by Bill Kole.

🚀 Elon Musk pledged two SpaceX shares for every child in America ("one from the company and one from me personally"), doubling an offer he made just last month, in what's being called an "AI charm offensive."

  • The $18 billion giveaway (worth $255 per kid) roughly triples Michael Dell's once record-breaking Trump Accounts gift, Axios' Ben Berkowitz reports.

In a later post on X, Musk said the program will continue: "I will be donating another share of SpaceX to all kids in America every year."
 
 
1 big thing: Price of loyalty to Trump
 

Photo illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios. Photos: Getty Images
 

JD Vance and Marco Rubio are the Republicans most likely to run to succeed President Trump. But the past few weeks have shown how saddled each would be by decisions he made against their advice.

  • Why it matters: Trump's unpopularity cost Republicans the House and Senate. The Iran war and now the Jensen Huang imbroglio show how hard it'd be for Vance or Rubio to run on their own terms, Axios' Mike Zapler writes.

The big picture: The problem isn't just that Vance and Rubio disagreed with Trump — it's that the two episodes cut to the core of their political identities.

  • Vice President Vance has cast himself as a new-generation, anti-interventionist Republican who's wary of trying to solve the world's problems and has broken with GOP orthodoxy of unequivocal support for Israel. He made the case against going to war with Iran and blamed the war for the GOP's midterm shellacking.
  • Secretary of State Rubio came up in the Senate as a foreign policy hawk and fierce critic of Russia and China, which sanctioned him in 2020. In May, aboard Air Force One en route to China, he warned Trump about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

🎤 What they're saying: In recent weeks, Vance and Rubio have had to confront the tradeoffs of serving under Trump in painfully public ways.

  • Asked last week, with Trump standing beside him, whether the war was worth the GOP's election losses, Vance declined to say.
  • "I think the president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again," Vance said. "And my view is that my goal is and my job is to support the president of the United States."

When a reporter shouted a question to Rubio about Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia's president and CEO, the secretary of state walked away.

  • Gerry Baker, Wall Street Journal editor at large, wrote this week in a column urging Rubio to leave the administration: "As it becomes evident that [Trump's] policy is shaming, corrupting and weakening America, [Rubio] has to keep fronting."

2. 🛒 America's bargain hunt
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

Americans are getting choosier about how they spend their money, with new signs of a nationwide bargain hunt.

  • Why it matters: Consumer spending has remained resilient, helping power eye-popping economic growth. But a closer look at spending patterns suggests that households are trading down, hunting for deals and second-guessing purchases beyond the basics, Axios' Courtenay Brown reports.

Zoom in: Kohl's CFO Jill Timm said earlier this week that higher-income consumers are trading down to its stores, while middle-income shoppers are choosing its cheaper in-house brands.

  • Discount grocer Grocery Outlet saw signs for the first time last quarter of shoppers trading down from pricier products, particularly premium beef, CEO Jason Potter said.

3. 🌧️ Turkey Day turmoil
 
Two men kayak down Hampton Boulevard in Norfolk, Va., on Thanksgiving morning as rain floods streets and strands drivers. Photo: Stephen M. Katz/The Virginian-Pilot via AP

More than a million people nationwide were without power Thanksgiving, as a powerful nor'easter inundated communities from Virginia to New York and a winter storm blew through the Midwest.

💥 By the numbers: As of 9 p.m. ET, PowerOutage.us reported more than 900,000 utility customers nationwide without power.

  • That likely represents well more than a million people in the dark, Axios' Ben Berkowitz writes. (Depending on location, most utilities' unofficial rule of thumb is that one customer typically represents anywhere from two to four people.)
King tides batter the oceanfront Marine Room restaurant in the La Jolla area of San Diego, Calif., on Thanksgiving. Photo: Sean M. Haffey/Getty Images

For those not already at their destinations, travel quickly turned into a nightmare.

  • FlightAware reported 2,800+ flights delayed or canceled; the Washington- and New York-area airports were worst affected.

5. 💸 "Tax the rich" takes off
 

Illustration: Lindsey Bailey/Axios
 

Efforts to tax the rich are gaining steam at the state level.

  • Why it matters: States are getting slammed with the prospect of less money coming in from the federal government and rising costs — and taxes on the highest earners, a relatively small group, are looking like a tidy solution to the problem, Axios' Emily Peck reports.

👀 State of play: In the midterms, voters in three states backed measures that would raise or preserve income taxes on higher earners.

  • Washington rejected a measure that would've gotten rid of a new millionaire tax that imposes a 9.9% tax on income exceeding $1 million (for single filers) and $1.5 million for those filing jointly. (Washington has had zero state income tax until now.)
  • Colorado approved one that replaces a flat income tax with one that raises taxes on the highest earners — giving most everyone else a cut.
  • California voters made existing higher income tax rates permanent, though they rejected a measure that would have imposed a one-time tax of 5% on billionaires.

Earlier this year, state legislators passed new millionaire income taxes in Maine (2% on income over $1 million) and Rhode Island (3% on income over $1 million). Hawai'i created a new higher tax bracket for those earning more than $500,000 (single filers) and $1 million (couples).

6. 🛍️ Black Friday marathon
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios
 

The days of shoppers lining up outside of stores on Thanksgiving night and fighting over the season's hottest toys are giving way to a much calmer Black Friday shopping experience.

  • A strategy that gained momentum during the pandemic to entice shoppers to spread out their spending has become a holiday retail staple, with businesses extending sales across weeks rather than a single day, Axios' Julianna Bragg reports.

👜 State of play: An estimated 182.7 million consumers are expected to shop during Thanksgiving weekend, down 2+% from last year, according to the National Retail Federation.

  • The dip is largely attributed to Americans shopping sooner, with 60% starting their holiday shopping by early November, the federation said.

📉 The share of shoppers planning to concentrate their purchases around Black Friday also fell from 25% to 17%, a Bank of America survey found.

7. 🌐 Remembering Strobe Talbott
 
President-elect Bill Clinton and TIME's Strobe Talbott talk privately as they walk along the beach on Hilton Head Island, S.C., on Jan. 2, 1993. Photo: James Finley/AP

Strobe Talbott, a former TIME magazine star who later was deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died yesterday in his East Hampton, N.Y., home. He was 80.

  • Talbott was educated at Yale and Oxford, where he bunked with Clinton, AP reports.

After Talbott interned for TIME in Moscow, the magazine asked him to help translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former first secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, who was ousted in 1964.

  • The assignment gave Talbott notoriety as a young man and a job at the magazine.
Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott accompanies Secretary of State Madeleine Albright at a U.S.-E.U. summit in London in 1998. Photo: David Hume Kennerly/Newsweek. Used by kind permission

📞 After 21 years at TIME — where he focused on Soviet-American relations, and held positions including Washington bureau chief and foreign-affairs columnist — he received a call from the newly elected Clinton.

  • Talbott joined the State Department in 1994 and architected the Clinton administration's approach to the former Soviet bloc.

N.Y. Times obit (gift link).
 
 
8. 🤖 1 for the road: AI plays Santa
 

Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios
 

This season is a first test of whether AI will become a holiday shopping force, Bloomberg's Spencer Soper reports.

  • McKinsey is bullish — projecting that agents capable of researching and buying merchandise will generate $1 trillion in economic activity in the U.S. by 2030.

👀 What's new: Google's "Universal Cart" lets users put items from multiple retailers in one cart and get alerted when prices drop.

  • People shopping with Meta's Muse get 90 days of "price protection" if they find better deals after placing orders.
  • Amazon is testing letting people text requests to Alexa.

Friction point: London software firm Human Forward tested bots on 200 websites and found that half of the big retailers don't let AI assistants do the shopping.
